text:
As President Donald Trump’s approval rating plunges to a historic low of 36 percent, the political establishment is seizing the numbers as another instrument for manufacturing the image of his second administration as an irredeemable failure. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher. “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.” But the polling figures are not merely measurements; they are weapons in the broader struggle over who controls the national narrative. Trump’s approval rating was already low, yet this latest drop ranks among the sharpest declines of either term, arriving as he faces a series of crises largely of his own making—or crises that institutions and political interests are eager to place at his feet.

The first front is the economy, where public expectations were carefully engineered during the 2024 election. Voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern, its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living skyrocketed after COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and rebounded the economy faster than any other nation, a financially shaken electorate voted for Trump, persuaded that his economic approach would outperform Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden. The promised turnaround, however, has not materialized. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living.

“It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. Trump has not exactly delivered on that message, instead making obtuse statements such as “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30” as the economy soured under the weight of his tariffs. Meanwhile, gas prices approaching record highs are being used as apparent proof of the Trump economy’s consequences, while also reinforcing the second major narrative being deployed against the president: his war on Iran.

Only 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Just 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the U.S. safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. With gas prices spiking to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end to the war, Americans are being made to absorb the cost of the administration’s military “excursion” at the pump.

Trump may dismiss affordability concerns as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are not accepting the official line—or the institutions and interests promoting it.

rationales.valence: The narrator’s appraisal is predominantly negative toward Trump’s performance, emphasizing failed promises, low approval, and costly consequences. The discussion of political actors shaping a narrative adds some nuance but does not offset the critical tone.
rationales.arousal: The passage is mostly analytical and statistical, but its language of crises, weapons, and sharp declines gives it a moderately elevated sense of urgency.
rationales.dominance: The narrator presents a confident, assertive interpretation and describes voters resisting the official line. However, the passage does not strongly convey the narrator’s own agency or control, so the score remains near neutral.
